iPATH applied-health-services human–LLM qualitative-analysis study; two task-specific workflows on one 12-FQHC comparative-case-study corpus. It cites LLooM/CollabCoder and prior human–LLM coding/theme-comparison studies but reports a distinct applied implementation and evaluation.

Propose a model- and task-agnostic framework for designing rigorous task-specific human–LLM qualitative-analysis methods and demonstrate it in two real-world tasks within a multi-site diabetes-care study.
not reported

Comparative case study using qualitative synthesis for actionable cross-site feedback and deductive qualitative coding to refine a practice-transformation intervention; qualitative rigor is evaluated against task-specific grounding, theory/data integration, research-question fit, significance, and practitioner usefulness rather than a single gold standard.
not reported
Human-LLM framework combining qualitative synthesis of researcher summaries and deductive coding to refine an intervention.

Researchers first perform each task manually on a small sample, decompose it into human and model subtasks, compare manual and LLM-assisted outputs at small scale, and then scale the selected workflow. Task 1 organizes researcher-authored site-summary bullets into themes before human synthesis. Task 2 uses researcher-developed subquestions, embedding retrieval, quote-grounded LLM summaries, automated quotation verification/deduplication, LLM relevance sorting, and human contextual interpretation across 167 transcripts.

Task 1 asks ChatGPT-4o to preserve and group site-summary bullets into categorical themes with a miscellaneous category, then prompts o1 to synthesize using the task goal, domain definitions, and four manual few-shot examples. Task 2 asks quote-grounded questions over RAG excerpts; every example-bearing subquestion is paired with a no-example version and a counter-perspective barriers question; outputs contain three to five summary/quote bullets and are later sorted by an LLM judge.

No agents are defined. ChatGPT-4o performs thematic organization, RAG-based quote-grounded coding, and relevance sorting; o1 performs Task 1 cross-site synthesis; text-embedding-3-large and Qdrant retrieve excerpts.

Qualitative researchers define goals and output formats, manually perform small samples, author site summaries and code/subquestion frameworks, compare manual with assisted outputs, revise themes, validate and contextualize quotes, revisit transcripts, interpret results, and retain responsibility for final syntheses and intervention decisions; computer scientists implement secure task-specific pipelines.
not reported

Task 1 thematic groupings and draft cross-site syntheses for 22 domains; Task 2 a 19-code by 12-site matrix whose cells contain about 30 summary-statement/supporting-quote bullets, plus source-interview identifiers
not reported

Task 1 instructs the model not to alter original bullet points and retains a miscellaneous category. Task 2 requires an illustrative quotation for every statement, records the source interview, returns retrieved excerpts, removes duplicate quotes, and uses a Python script to verify that every quoted string occurs in the transcripts; researchers revisit original transcripts for context.
not reported

Manual no-LLM performance of the same tasks: two researchers cross over manual versus assisted synthesis for two comparable Task 1 domains; Task 2 compares the assisted method with manual coding of six interviews from two sites across four codes of different complexity. Multiple candidate model families were explored during workflow development.
not reported

Task 1 small-scale comparison covers two researchers and two domains; Task 2 small-scale comparison covers six interviews, two sites, and four codes. Repeated stochastic runs, random seeds, and per-configuration run counts are not reported.
not reported

No automatic metric is used to establish qualitative interpretive quality. The workflow uses embedding similarity thresholds (initially 0.4, lowered to 0.3), exact quotation validation/deduplication, and descriptive time comparisons; the authors explicitly reject agreement/overlap as sufficient gold-standard measures for these tasks.
not reported in this track's verified extraction

Task 1 uses a two-researcher crossed comparison: each researcher manually synthesizes one of two similar domains and uses LLM outputs for the other, then compares quality and timing. Task 2 compares manual with assisted analysis on six interviews from two sites and four codes, followed by research-team assessment against task-specific rigor and utility criteria; blinding and independent external evaluation are not reported.
not reported

Task 1 explicitly includes two qualitative researchers. Task 2 includes at least one qualitative researcher and team discussion, but the exact evaluator count and individual expertise are not fully enumerated; the collaboration spans qualitative, health-services, clinical, and computer-science expertise.
not reported
not reported

not reported; the authors argue that inter-rater reliability or thematic overlap cannot by itself capture interpretive depth and use expected variation between competent human researchers as a practical benchmark

No inferential test, confidence interval, or formal uncertainty analysis is reported; evaluation is qualitative and descriptive, with per-researcher time reductions and projected coding-time calculations.
not reported

For Task 1, LLM organization was comparable to human grouping, but model syntheses lacked actionable nuance, novelty judgment, and contextual correction; researchers retained interpretive control. Assisted synthesis reduced time by 30% for one researcher and 55% for the other. For Task 2, model and human findings were often complementary, but RAG fragmentation caused tangential retrieval, loss of perspective, and overgeneralization; quote/source access let researchers validate and contextualize outputs. The scaled workflow integrated 167 interviews across 19 practice areas into intervention refinements that the team judged infeasible on the deadline by manual coding alone.
not reported

Task 1 time fell by 30% and 55% for the two researchers in the small comparison. Manual Task 2 coding took 20 hours for three transcripts across four codes; the authors project approximately 310 hours for one site and 93 full-time workweeks for all 12 sites at that observed pace. Monetary cost is not reported; ChatGPT-4o was chosen over o1 for Task 2 based on cost and efficiency.
not reported

Advarra IRB approval (Pro00071432) and informed consent are reported. High-risk medical data were processed through Stanford SecureGPT; commercial/open tools were rejected when security, institutional approval, scale, cost, or opacity were unsuitable. Data remain restricted for confidentiality, and the discussion addresses bias, decontextualization, reflexivity, transparency, and loss of researcher familiarity.
not reported in this track's verified extraction

The paper reports the task framework, models, temperature, retrieval thresholds, output structure, and workflow diagrams; supplementary sections are cited for domains, code definitions, prompts, subquestions, and interface details. Code is publicly identified as github.com/sronaghi/LLMsinQualAnalysis. Data are restricted, and dated model snapshots, random seeds, complete run logs, and the cited supplement were not present in the inspected 20-page PDF.
not reported

LLM outputs can lack nuance, novelty judgment, perspective, and context; RAG can fragment data and surface tangential excerpts; models may overfit examples and favor positive accounts; large-team/site variation changes model behavior; researchers may lose data familiarity if reading is delegated; existing commercial/open tools can be insecure, expensive, opaque, inflexible, or unable to handle the corpus; and current models lack long-context/domain reasoning needed for direct insight generation.
not reported
Only primary preprint HTML/abstract-level verification was completed; do not use for detailed quantitative synthesis without renewed full-text extraction.

The small-scale comparisons cover only two Task 1 domains and six Task 2 interviews/four codes, use participating researchers rather than blinded independent evaluators, and report no formal uncertainty or repeated-run stability. Task-specific sufficiency was determined by the same interdisciplinary team developing the workflow. Efficiency projections extrapolate one observed manual rate, and proprietary model snapshots are not dated.

Extends task-specific human–AI collaboration principles and prior human-versus-LLM qualitative coding/theme studies by embedding secure LLM workflows in a real, large multi-site applied-health study. It uses LLooM/CollabCoder and earlier evaluation work as methodological context but contributes distinct iPATH workflows and outcomes.

values: Direct evidence for human-centered task decomposition, plurality-aware evaluation, quote/source provenance, context-loss diagnostics, secure sensitive-data processing, workflow-specific efficiency measurement, and why agreement/overlap metrics cannot substitute for interpretive quality in large-scale qualitative analysis.
Novelty and methodological-context check for the proposed ARR project.
